sections.b: Colossians answers a teaching at Colossae that offered fullness through rules about food and days, fasting, visions and the worship of angels. Its reply is Christ: the image of the unseen God in whom all things were created and reconciled (1:15-20), in whom all the fullness of deity lives bodily (2:9), and in whom believers are already made full (2:10). It ends with the new life of love, a household code and greetings shared with Philemon.

common: Most readers take 1:15-20 as one of the New Testament's highest statements about Christ.
uncommon: Morna Hooker's essay 'Were There False Teachers in Colossae?' (1973) is cited for reading the letter as encouragement for a young church rather than a reply to one definite group of false teachers.

sections.b: Colossae was a small Phrygian town in the Lycus valley, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Its church was founded by Epaphras, a local man (Colossians 1:7; 4:12), and Paul had never visited it (2:1). It met in houses, including Philemon's, and its members included the slave Onesimus (4:9). Tacitus records an earthquake that overthrew Laodicea in AD 60; Eusebius, as Lightfoot reports, dated a quake a few years later and included Colossae. The town faded in importance. Pamukkale University surveyed the site from 2021 and began excavating in 2025, reporting about 60 rock-cut tombs in one burial ground that year.

sections.h: Firstborn of creation, firstborn from the dead
sections.b: Colossians 1:15 calls Christ 'the firstborn of all creation' and 1:18 'the firstborn from the dead'. Drawing on the Old Testament sense of firstborn as rank and heir (Exodus 4:22; Psalm 89:27), the hymn gives the reason: in him all things were created. In the 300s Arius read the word as 'first created' and Athanasius as rank, saying that 'firstborn' is used 'because of brethren', while the Son is 'other than the whole creation'. Jehovah's Witnesses today follow a reading like Arius'.

common: 'Firstborn' in Colossians 1:15 means first in rank and heir of all things, not the first creature.
uncommon: Jehovah's Witnesses read 'firstborn of all creation' as 'the first creation by Jehovah God'.

sections.h: Christ the image, and the new self renewed in it
sections.b: Colossians 1:15 calls Christ 'the image of the God who cannot be seen', using the Greek of Genesis 1:26-27 and of Jewish praise of Wisdom (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). Colossians 3:10 then says the new self is 'being made new in knowledge, to match the image of the one who created it'. The restored human image is shaped after Christ, who is the image.

Colossians speaks of 'the kingdom of the Son of his love' (1:13), then describes that Son as the image of God, firstborn of all creation, the one in whom, through whom and for whom all things were made, and in whom all the fullness of deity lives bodily (1:15-20; 2:9). These verses became central in the fourth-century debate over whether the Son is a creature or 'begotten not made' (Nicaea, 325).

sections.h: All things created in him, through him, for him
sections.b: Colossians 1:16-17 says that all things in heaven and on earth, seen and unseen, were created in Christ, through him and for him, and that all things hold together in him. Christ is not only the agent of creation (1 Corinthians 8:6; John 1:3) but its goal.

Much of what Colossians 1:15-20 says of Christ was said of Wisdom: present at creation (Proverbs 8:22-31), 'an image of his goodness' (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). Colossians 2:3 adds that 'all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' are hidden in Christ, against teachers who offered a wisdom of rules and visions (2:23).

sections.h: Created, headed and paraded: the powers in Colossians
sections.b: Colossians names 'thrones, lordships, rulers and authorities' as things created in Christ (1:16), says that Christ is the head of every ruler and authority (2:10), and pictures them stripped and led in his victory parade at the cross (2:15). The letter's readers, tempted toward 'the worship of angels' (2:18), are told that no such power stands between them and God.

Colossians links 'the basic elements of the world' with 'philosophy', 'human tradition' (2:8), and with rules such as 'Do not take hold! Do not taste! Do not even touch!' (2:20-21). The believers 'died with Christ' and left the elements behind. As in Galatians, readers divide between elementary teachings, the physical elements, and spirits connected with them.

Colossians never names its opponents. Pieced together from 2:8-23, their teaching involved 'philosophy' and tradition, the elements of the world, food and drink, festivals, new moons and Sabbaths, fasting ('self-humbling'), 'the worship of angels', visions, and ascetic rules. Proposals range from Jewish mystical piety (Francis) and Essene-like Judaism (Lightfoot) to a local mix of folk religion, Judaism and Christianity (Arnold), Epicurean philosophy (DeWitt), or no definite group of false teachers at all (Hooker).

uncommon: Norman DeWitt linked the Colossian 'philosophy' and 'elements' to Epicurean thought.

sections.h: Christ in you, the hope of glory
sections.b: Colossians calls the mystery 'kept hidden from the ages and from the generations, but now ... made plain to his saints' (1:26), and defines it as 'Christ in you, the hope of glory' (1:27), 'God's mystery, that is, Christ' (2:2), and 'the mystery of Christ' that Paul is in chains for (4:3). The mystery is open to all, not to a few initiates.

sections.h: Buried and raised with him; circumcision without hands
sections.b: Colossians 2:11-12 links the 'circumcision not done by human hands' with being 'buried with him' in baptism and 'raised with him, through faith in God's working'. Unlike Romans 6:5, the rising is already past (also 3:1). Reformed teaching uses the link between circumcision and baptism to support infant baptism (Heidelberg Catechism 74); Baptists stress the words 'through faith'; the Catholic Catechism calls baptism 'that "circumcision of Christ"' (527).

sections.h: A circumcision not done by hands
sections.b: Colossians 2:11 says believers 'received circumcision, one not done by human hands', the 'circumcision of Christ', in the stripping off of 'the body of the flesh'. The idea comes from the Torah's call to circumcise the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6). Gentile believers lacked nothing that circumcision promised (2:13). Colossians 3:11 still names 'circumcised and uncircumcised' as a difference that no longer ranks people in Christ.

sections.h: A shadow of what is to come (Colossians 2:16-17)
sections.b: Colossians tells Gentile believers not to let anyone judge them about 'a festival, a new moon or Sabbaths', the standard list of Israel's holy times, which are 'the shadow of what is to come', while 'the body is Christ's'. The Augsburg Confession quotes the passage and says 'Scripture has abrogated the Sabbath-day'; the Westminster Confession holds that the Sabbath moved to the Lord's Day as 'the Christian Sabbath'; Seventh-day Adventist scholars such as Ron du Preez read the 'sabbaths' here as Israel's ceremonial sabbaths, not the weekly one.

sections.h: Eating and drinking, and 'Do not taste'
sections.b: Colossians 2:16 forbids anyone to judge the believers 'in eating or drinking', and 2:21-22 mocks rules like 'Do not take hold! Do not taste! Do not even touch!' as human commandments (echoing Isaiah 29:13 as quoted in Mark 7:7). The concern seems to include fasting and abstinence beyond the Torah's own food laws.

Colossians warns against one who 'delights in self-humbling and in the worship of angels'. The phrase may mean worship directed to angels (calling on them for help, which a later council at Laodicea forbade) or the angels' own worship, which visionaries hoped to join in heaven. Colossians 1:16 had already placed every angelic rank among the things created in Christ.

Colossians 3:18-4:1 is the shortest New Testament household code. It addresses wives, husbands, children, fathers, slaves and masters in turn, each 'in the Lord', the same three pairs Aristotle called 'the primary and smallest parts of the household'. It runs parallel to Ephesians 5:22-6:9 but is much shorter. Its longest section is to slaves, and its word to masters ('you too have a Lord in heaven') is set beside the letter to Philemon, carried with it.

Colossians speaks to slaves as members of the church, promises them the inheritance (3:24) and says the Lord shows no favoritism (3:25); it tells masters to give their slaves 'what is just and what is equal' (4:1). It does not call for an end to slavery. The same letter introduces Onesimus, a slave, as 'the faithful and beloved brother' (4:9).
Colossians 4:7-8 sends Tychicus with news and encouragement, in words almost identical to Ephesians 6:21-22, adding that he is a 'fellow slave in the Lord'. He travels with Onesimus (4:9).

Colossians 4:9 introduces Onesimus to the church as 'the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you', sent with Tychicus to bring news. Nothing is said of his slavery or his past; the letter to Philemon tells that side.

Colossians names Laodicea four times: Paul struggles for the believers there (2:1), Epaphras works for them (4:13), the brothers there and Nympha's house church are greeted (4:15), and the letters are to be exchanged, the Colossians reading 'the one from Laodicea' (4:16). Tacitus says an earthquake overthrew Laodicea in AD 60 and that the city rebuilt from its own resources.

Colossians 4:16 shows Paul's letters being read in one church and passed to another, and mentions a letter 'from Laodicea' that is lost, or is Ephesians or Philemon under another name. A Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans', made from phrases of Philippians, was copied in many Latin Bibles but is held as Scripture by no church.

sections.h: The bill nailed to the cross
sections.b: Colossians pictures the cross in three ways: peace made 'through the blood of his cross' (1:20), a handwritten bill of debt wiped away and nailed to the cross (2:14), and the rulers and authorities stripped and led in a victory parade (2:15). The last picture is a main text for the 'Christus Victor' view of the atonement.

Colossians 4:15 greets 'Nympha, and the church that meets in her house' in Laodicea, a woman hosting a congregation. Some manuscripts make the name a man's, Nymphas, with 'his house'. Philemon 2 names another house church in Colossae itself.

sections.h: Psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit
sections.b: Colossians 3:16 makes singing a way of teaching and warning one another and of letting the word of Christ live richly in the church. The same three words appear in Ephesians 5:19. The hymn of 1:15-20 may be an example of what the church sang.

Paul writes from prison that he is glad in his sufferings for the Colossians and that he is 'filling up' in his own flesh 'what is still missing from Christ's hardships', for the sake of Christ's body, the church. The verse has been read in very different ways. Catholic teaching sees in it the value of suffering joined to Christ's (Salvifici Doloris, 1984). John Chrysostom read the sufferings as Christ's own, borne in Paul. Calvin, adopting Augustine's words, denied that any martyr's blood is shed for the forgiveness of sins, and read the verse as the afflictions the Father appointed for Christ's body. The 'Where Christians differ' card on Colossians 1 sets the views side by side.

sections.h: Head of the body, and the household code
sections.b: Colossians uses 'head' first of Christ: he is 'the head of the body, the church' (1:18), 'the head of every ruler and authority' (2:10), and the head from whom the whole body grows (2:19). In the household code it does not use 'head' for the husband, as Ephesians 5:23 does; it tells wives to submit to their husbands 'as is proper in the Lord' and husbands to love their wives and not turn bitter against them (3:18-19). The churches' teaching on headship in marriage is set out on the card on Ephesians 5.

Colossians opens 'Paul ... and Timothy our brother' (1:1), as 2 Corinthians, Philippians and Philemon do, but then speaks in Paul's voice. Because the letter's style differs from Paul's other letters, some scholars think Timothy had a hand in writing it: Eduard Schweizer proposed joint authorship, and James Dunn's commentary is cited for the possibility that Timothy was the secretary.

Colossians 4:14 is the only place that says Luke was a doctor. He sends greetings with Demas, as in Philemon 24, and 2 Timothy 4:11 says 'Luke is the only one with me'. Irenaeus, about AD 180, wrote that 'Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him'.

Colossians 4:10 sends greetings from 'Mark, Barnabas's cousin', and tells the church to welcome him if he comes. The Mark who had left Paul and Barnabas in Pamphylia (Acts 13:13; Acts 15:37-39) is with Paul again, as in Philemon 24 and 2 Timothy 4:11. Papias, quoted by Eusebius, linked a Mark with Peter as his interpreter, and tradition links him with the Gospel of Mark.

Colossians 4:10 names Mark as 'Barnabas's cousin' (anepsios, not 'nephew'), which explains why Barnabas took Mark's side when Paul refused to take him again (Acts 15:37-39). The name assumes the Colossians knew who Barnabas was.
